name: Density
kicker: Mass packed into a given space · Why ice floats and rocks sink
dates: Archimedes’ crown test, 3rd century BCE (traditional story)
briefing: Density tells you how much mass is packed into a given space: a brick and a block of foam the same size have very different densities. You find it by dividing an object’s mass by its volume, and anything less dense than water, like a block of wood, floats on it. Water itself is a strange case: it is densest at about 4 °C, and ice is less dense than liquid water, which is why ice cubes float.
answerHtml: density (accept mass density; prompt on specific gravity, relative density, or rho; do not accept “mass” or “volume”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Henry Cavendish’s 1798 experiment, often described as “weighing the world,” found Earth’s average value of this quantity to be about five and a half times that of water. Earth has the highest value of this quantity of any planet in the solar system.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, found by dividing an object’s mass by its volume.

tossups.p: A Galileo thermometer works because its glass bulbs rise or sink as this property of the liquid around them changes with temperature. Each bulb carries a small tag marked with a temperature.
tossups.r: Of the planets, only Saturn has a lower average value of this property than water. For 10 points, name this property, measured in grams per cubic centimeter.

tossups.p: Osmium has the highest value of this property of any element, just ahead of iridium, while lithium has the lowest value of any metal and can even float on water. A block of osmium has about twice the mass of a lead block the same size.
tossups.r: Objects with more of it than water sink. For 10 points, name this property, equal to mass per unit volume.

tossups.p: According to a story told by the Roman writer Vitruvius [“vih-TROO-vee-us”], Archimedes [“ar-kih-MEE-deez”] figured out how to test whether King Hiero’s [“HY-er-ohz”] crown was pure gold while stepping into a bath, then ran home shouting “Eureka!”
tossups.r: He realized that the water pushed aside would reveal the crown’s volume. For 10 points, name this property, mass divided by volume, that showed whether the crown was pure gold.

tossups.p: Lakes freeze from the top down partly because liquid water reaches its greatest value of this property at about 4 °C, so the water at the bottom of a deep lake stays near that temperature all winter.
tossups.r: Ice floats because it has less of this property than liquid water. For 10 points, name this property, an object’s mass divided by its volume.

tossups.p: Submarines dive and surface by flooding or emptying ballast tanks, which changes their overall value of this quantity compared with the seawater around them. Many fish do the same job by adjusting the gas in a swim bladder.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity whose value for pure water is 1 gram per cubic centimeter.

tossups.p: A hydrometer floats higher in liquids that have more of this property, so the mark on its stem at the surface tells the value. Dividing this property of a substance by that of water gives a unitless number called specific gravity.
tossups.r: Things with less of it than water float. For 10 points, name this property calculated as mass divided by volume.

tossups.p: An iron or lead cannonball floats on liquid mercury, because mercury has a greater value of this property than either metal. Gold, however, sinks in mercury. Mercury has about 13.5 times as much of this property as water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, symbolized by the Greek letter rho, which equals mass divided by volume.

tossups.p: Very salty water has more of this property than fresh water, which is why swimmers float so easily in the Dead Sea and why a raw egg that sinks in tap water can float in strong salt water.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this property, which tells whether an object will sink or float in a liquid.

tossups.p: In the North Atlantic, cold, salty seawater sinks because it has a high value of this quantity, helping drive a slow, worldwide loop of deep ocean currents called the thermohaline circulation. Antarctic Bottom Water has the highest value of this quantity of any large mass of ocean water.
tossups.r: Warm air rises for the opposite reason. For 10 points, name this quantity, mass per unit volume.

tossups.p: A neutron star packs more mass than the Sun into a ball about the size of a city, giving it an enormous value of this quantity. A white dwarf has a smaller but still huge value of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity found by dividing an object’s mass by its volume.

tossups.p: A can of regular soda usually sinks in a tank of water while a can of diet soda floats, because the sugar dissolved in regular soda raises this property.
tossups.r: A classroom “tower” stacks honey, water, and oil in layers by this property. For 10 points, name this property, mass divided by volume.

tossups.p: Water has roughly 800 times as much of this quantity as air at sea level. At a fixed pressure, heating a gas lowers this quantity, which is why a hot-air balloon rises through the cooler air around it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, an object’s mass per unit volume, often given in grams per cubic centimeter.

tossups.p: Hydrogen bonds lock frozen water molecules into an open, six-sided pattern with lots of empty space, so water expands by about nine percent when it freezes and its value of this property drops.
tossups.r: That is why ice floats. For 10 points, name this property, an object’s mass divided by its volume.

tossups.p: The kilogram was first based on the mass of one liter of water, so water’s value of this quantity was set at one kilogram per liter. Seawater has slightly more of this quantity than fresh water.
tossups.r: To find this quantity for a rock, measure its volume by how much water it pushes aside, then divide its mass by that volume. For 10 points, name this quantity.

trap.title: Not mass, not volume
trap.body: This quantity is built from two others, mass and volume, and tossups mention both, so players blurt one of them. Mass is how much matter an object has and volume is how much space it takes up; this answer is the ratio between them. Buoyancy, the upward push of a fluid, shows up in the same questions but is a separate answer, and “specific gravity” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Mass divided by volume, grams per cubic centimeter, rho, floating and sinking, and ice floating point to this answer. If the question asks for “this upward force,” say buoyancy instead.
trap.line: Real answer line: density (accept mass density; prompt on specific gravity, relative density, or rho; do not accept “mass” or “volume”)
